subject: professional-responsibility
title: Counsel of the Fairy Court
kicker: Loyalty. Candor. A little fairy dust.
intro: A study path through professional duties, cases, hypothetical problems, and cumulative review.
scope: Explore admission, client formation, confidentiality, conflicts, advocacy, judicial conduct, prosecution, and public service. The ABA Model Rules supply the baseline; jurisdictions may adopt different language. Each topic gives the governing test and a fresh application.

sections.title: The profession & its rulemakers
sections.tagline: The right rule begins with the right jurisdiction.

points.title: Several systems can apply
points.text: Professional discipline, civil liability, procedural sanctions, and criminal law are **different systems**. The ABA Model Rules are a model, not automatically binding law everywhere. A violation does not by itself create a malpractice claim, though it may be evidence of breach under applicable law.

points.title: Authority is not choice of law
points.text: Rule 8.5 can expose an admitted lawyer to home-jurisdiction discipline for conduct elsewhere, and an outside lawyer to local authority for offering services there. For a **pending tribunal matter**, generally use the tribunal jurisdiction’s rules unless its rules say otherwise. Other conduct follows the location or **predominant effect**, with the stated reasonable-belief safe harbor.

points.title: Candor and reporting
points.text: Rule 8.1 prohibits knowing material falsehoods and specified nondisclosure in admission or discipline matters, subject to protected confidentiality and constitutional rights. Rule 8.3 generally requires reporting **known violations raising a substantial question** about honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness, but excludes information protected by Rule 1.6 and specified assistance-program information.

sections.example: Rowan practices in the Oak Court but handles a pending case in the Willow Court. Two authorities may be able to discipline him. Which conduct rules apply is a separate question that starts with the tribunal rule, not simply where he keeps his desk.
tips: Identify the **type of consequence** the question asks about.
Do not confuse **who can discipline** with **which rule governs**.

terms.definition: Authority to investigate and discipline a lawyer.
The method for choosing the applicable jurisdiction’s conduct rules.
The main place where conduct has its consequences, relevant to Rule 8.5’s nontribunal analysis.

sections.comicCaption: The council writes the rules; each jurisdiction decides which rules bind its lawyers.

sections.title: Who may practice & who must supervise
sections.tagline: A border is a legal fact, even when the work is remote.

points.title: Authorization is local
points.text: Rule 5.5 prohibits unauthorized practice and assisting it. Admission somewhere is **not a universal license**. Temporary-service exceptions have conditions: association with actively participating local counsel, litigation or ADR-related authority, or qualifying work reasonably related to the home practice.

points.title: Presence and permission differ
points.text: A physical office is not the only relevant contact. A continuous local practice or holding out as locally admitted can trigger restrictions. Separate temporary practice, in-house authority, federal authorization, and **pro hac vice** requirements. Modern local rules may differ from older cases.

points.title: Delegation keeps responsibility
points.text: Rule 5.3 requires reasonable systems and supervision so nonlawyer assistance is compatible with professional obligations; ordering, ratifying, or failing to remedy specified known misconduct can create responsibility. Rule 5.7 can extend duties to **law-related services** where separation and adequate warnings are absent.

sections.example: Thistle asks a clerk to organize documents, supplies confidentiality instructions, and checks the work. That is different from telling an unsupervised clerk to choose the client’s legal strategy. Delegating a task does not transfer the lawyer’s duty.
tips: Find the **specific authorization**, not just a travel itinerary.
Supervision applies to useful outside assistance as well as people at the next desk.

terms.definition: Providing legal services without the authorization required in the relevant jurisdiction.
Permission to appear in a particular matter without general admission, subject to local requirements.
Services related to legal work that are not themselves prohibited legal practice when performed by a nonlawyer.

sections.comicCaption: A license opens the gate. Supervising lawyers remain responsible for the team’s work.

sections.title: The first consultation & client identity
sections.tagline: The relationship may start before the signature.

points.title: Conduct can create duties
points.text: An engagement letter clarifies the job but is not the only way to form a relationship. Legal advice, manifested assent, and reasonable reliance can matter under applicable law. **No payment** does not necessarily mean **no client**.

points.title: Prospective clients have protection
points.text: Under Rule 1.18, a person consulting about possible representation may be a **prospective client** even if no engagement follows. The lawyer generally cannot use or reveal consultation information except as Rule 1.9 allows. Not every unsolicited message creates that status; consider the circumstances and reasonable expectations.

points.title: Separate confidentiality from disqualification
points.text: Representation adverse to a prospective client in the same or substantially related matter can be barred when the lawyer received information that **could be significantly harmful**. Informed written consent by both affected persons or the rule’s limited-information, screening, no-fee, and notice pathway may permit representation.

sections.example: A merchant tells Rowan sensitive settlement priorities during a genuine consultation. Rowan declines the matter. He cannot treat those priorities as free intelligence for the opponent simply because no fee agreement was signed.
tips: Ask **whose interests you are undertaking to protect**.
A conflict restriction can have a narrower trigger than the duty to protect consultation information.

terms.definition: A person who consults a lawyer about possible representation in a matter.
Information capable of materially disadvantaging the prospective client in the relevant matter.
Procedures isolating a disqualified lawyer from a matter; effective only where the governing rule permits that solution.

sections.comicCaption: Before advice begins, identify the client and protect the prospective client’s information.

sections.title: Competence, malpractice & assistance
sections.tagline: Know which standard the problem is asking you to apply.

points.title: Competent service
points.text: Rule 1.1 requires **legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation** reasonably necessary for the matter. A lawyer can become competent through reasonable study or association; expertise is not always required at intake. Emergency help must stay within what is reasonably necessary when referral or consultation is impractical.

points.title: Civil malpractice
points.text: A negligence claim ordinarily asks about **duty, breach, causation, and damages**, with details controlled by local law. Proving an error is not enough if it did not cause the claimed loss. A bad outcome alone does not establish negligent work.

points.title: Constitutional assistance
points.text: Strickland ordinarily requires **deficient performance** and a **reasonable probability of a different result** sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome. This is not a simple ethics-rule checklist. Presumed-prejudice and structural-error doctrines are limited exceptions, not the default.

sections.example: Thistle accepts an unfamiliar but manageable boundary dispute, studies the governing law, and consults experienced counsel. Compare that with sending an unprepared advocate into a hearing. Novelty alone is not the violation; inadequate preparation can be.
tips: State the **duty and remedy** before deciding whether harm must be shown.
Do not infer deficient performance solely from losing the case.

terms.definition: The knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably needed for the service.
The required connection between a lawyer’s breach and the client’s legally recognized loss.
A reasonable probability that, without deficient performance, the proceeding’s result would have differed.

sections.comicCaption: Competence means preparation, skill, and asking for help when the matter demands it.

sections.title: Limited work & malpractice agreements
sections.tagline: Limit the task carefully; read the liability clause separately.

points.title: Rule 1.2(c): scope
points.text: A limited engagement must be **reasonable under the circumstances** and supported by **informed consent**. Explain excluded work, material risks, and alternatives. The Model Rule does not universally demand a writing, but another applicable requirement may. Competent work remains required inside the boundary.

points.title: Rule 1.8(h)(1): future liability
points.text: A prospective malpractice limitation is different. It requires the client to be **independently represented in making the agreement**. A signature, sophisticated client, or suggestion to consult another lawyer is not enough.

points.title: Rule 1.8(h)(2): existing claim
points.text: For settling a malpractice claim or potential claim with an unrepresented current or former client, provide **written advice about the desirability of independent counsel** and a **reasonable opportunity** to seek that advice. Actual retention is not required by this paragraph. Do not confuse it with the future-liability rule.

sections.example: Rowan agrees to review a lease’s wording without investigating the building, after explaining that reasonable limitation. A separate clause saying “I am never liable for my mistakes” raises a different rule. Clear scope does not erase responsibility for negligent work within it.
tips: Classify the agreement: **services, future liability, or existing claim**.
“You may hire a lawyer” is not **actual independent representation**.

terms.definition: Agreement after adequate explanation of material risks and reasonably available alternatives.
A reasonable, consented boundary on the legal services undertaken.
An agreement reducing responsibility for malpractice that has not yet occurred.

sections.comicCaption: Draw the boundary of a limited engagement clearly, with informed consent and a reasonable scope.

sections.title: Client choices & lawyer judgment
sections.tagline: Know who holds the decision.

points.title: Objectives belong to the client
points.text: Rule 1.2 requires adherence to the client’s decisions about **objectives**, with consultation about means. The client decides **whether to settle**. In a criminal case, after consultation, the client decides the plea, jury waiver, and whether to testify. Legal and procedural requirements still apply.

points.title: Strategy is not unlimited control
points.text: Counsel ordinarily exercises professional judgment about technical means and may select stronger appellate issues rather than raise every nonfrivolous point. But a competent defendant’s **express objective to maintain innocence** cannot be overridden by a concession of guilt merely because counsel thinks it tactically wise.

points.title: No assistance in crime or fraud
points.text: Rule 1.2(d) bars counseling or assisting conduct the lawyer **knows is criminal or fraudulent**. A lawyer may explain legal consequences and help make a good-faith effort to determine the law’s validity, scope, meaning, or application. Representation does not mean endorsement of the client’s views.

sections.example: Thistle believes a settlement is excellent, but her client rejects it. She must advise and explain, not secretly accept. In a separate appeal, she may use professional judgment to omit a weak argument while pursuing the authorized appeal.
tips: Separate **the client’s objective** from **the lawyer’s tactical means**.
A client’s instruction cannot authorize knowing assistance in fraud.

terms.definition: The end the client seeks from the representation.
The methods used to pursue an authorized objective, developed through consultation and professional judgment.
The client’s right to control decisions reserved to the client, including certain fundamental criminal-case choices.

sections.comicCaption: The client chooses the destination; counsel explains the routes and controls lawful technique.

sections.title: Diligence, communication & withdrawal
sections.tagline: Leaving a matter is also a professional act.

points.title: Move the matter and explain it
points.text: Rules 1.3 and 1.4 require **reasonable diligence**, promptness, meaningful consultation, timely status information, and enough explanation for informed client choices. Rule 3.2 requires reasonable efforts to expedite litigation consistent with client interests; delay solely to frustrate an opponent is not justified merely because a client wants it.

points.title: Required versus permitted departure
points.text: Rule 1.16 requires assessment of the representation and, in specified circumstances, withdrawal: legal or rule violations, material impairment, discharge, and specified continued client misuse after discussion. Permissive grounds include reasonable warning followed by substantial nonpayment, unreasonable burden, or certain fundamental disagreements. **A difficult client alone is not an automatic exit**.

points.title: Protect the transition
points.text: Comply with **tribunal permission or notice requirements** and continue if ordered despite good cause. On departure, take reasonable steps to protect the client: notice, time for new counsel, papers and property, and refunds of unearned fees or expenses. Confidentiality survives.

sections.example: Rowan has unpaid bills and wants to leave before a hearing. He must assess the grounds, give appropriate warning, seek required permission, and protect the client’s transition. Silently missing the hearing would not become proper withdrawal.
tips: A ground for withdrawal is not permission to **abandon the file**.
For an active court matter, check both the ethics rule and **the tribunal’s order**.

terms.definition: Reasonable prompt and committed attention to a client’s matter.
Circumstances requiring refusal or termination, subject to applicable tribunal requirements.
Circumstances allowing, but not automatically requiring, departure under the rule.

sections.comicCaption: Move diligently, communicate changes, and protect the client when representation ends.

sections.title: Confidentiality, privilege & work product
sections.tagline: Three protections. Three different questions.

points.title: Rule 1.6 is broad
points.text: The duty covers **information relating to representation**, whatever its source, not merely a client’s secret communication. Disclosure requires informed consent, implied authorization to carry out representation, or an applicable exception. Public availability alone does not erase the ethics duty.

points.title: Privilege is a proof protection
points.text: Attorney-client privilege generally protects **confidential communications for legal advice** against compelled disclosure, subject to governing law and exceptions. It does not cloak every underlying fact or physical item. **Work product** concerns litigation preparation and has its own scope and qualified protections.

points.title: Protect information in practice
points.text: Rule 1.6(c) requires **reasonable efforts** against unauthorized or inadvertent disclosure or access. Match safeguards to sensitivity and circumstances: careful recipients, access limits, secure systems, and supervision. An information-sharing tool does not supply client authorization by itself.

sections.example: Thistle learns a fact from a public record while handling a client’s case. It can relate to the representation and remain ethically protected even though no privileged communication created it. Before discussing it outside the representation, identify a legitimate disclosure basis.
tips: Ask whether the question concerns **voluntary disclosure**, **compelled testimony**, or **litigation preparation**.
A fictional nickname may still reveal a client when the surrounding details identify the matter.

terms.definition: The professional duty restricting use and disclosure of information related to representation.
A legal protection for qualifying confidential legal-advice communications against compelled disclosure.
Protection for qualifying litigation-preparation material; its rules differ from both privilege and ethical confidentiality.

sections.comicCaption: Keep information relating to representation secure; privilege and work product have separate tests.

sections.title: Disclosure exceptions & competing duties
sections.tagline: “May” and “must” change the answer.

points.title: Prevent serious harm
points.text: Model Rule 1.6(b)(1) **permits** disclosure to the extent reasonably believed necessary to prevent **reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm**. The danger need not result from a client crime or the lawyer’s services. Local rules can impose a different duty.

points.title: Financial harm has extra conditions
points.text: The crime-or-fraud financial/property exceptions require substantial injury and **use of the lawyer’s services** in furtherance. A completed past crime disclosed only to obtain defense advice does not automatically qualify. Other exceptions address ethics advice, certain self-defense needs, law or court orders, and limited conflict detection.

points.title: Use only what is needed
points.text: Permission is limited by **reasonable necessity**. Separate Rule 3.3 candor duties, which can require remedial disclosure despite Rule 1.6, from ordinary discretionary exceptions. Physical evidence cannot be unlawfully altered or concealed under Rule 3.4; protection of information does not immunize conduct.

sections.example: Rowan learns that a hidden structural defect poses a reasonably certain danger of serious injury. He analyzes the narrow protective disclosure allowed by the Model Rule. He does not publish the entire client file simply because one exception may permit a warning.
tips: Identify the **exception’s exact facts** before deciding disclosure is permitted.
After finding permission, ask **how much disclosure is reasonably necessary**.

terms.definition: A sufficiently concrete danger under the applicable exception; not necessarily a harm occurring at this instant.
Disclosure the rule allows, as distinct from a command to disclose.
A step to correct misconduct or false evidence; candor rules can require escalating action.

sections.comicCaption: A disclosure exception is a narrow gate. Check its trigger, purpose, and scope.

sections.title: Loyalty, former clients & consent
sections.tagline: A signature cannot cure every conflict.

points.title: Current-client conflicts
points.text: Rule 1.7 asks about **direct adversity** or a **significant risk of material limitation** from duties to someone else or the lawyer’s own interests. Consent works only if the lawyer reasonably believes competent and diligent service remains possible, the representation is lawful, it does not involve prohibited opposing claims in the same proceeding, and each affected client gives **informed consent confirmed in writing**.

points.title: Former-client matters
points.text: Rule 1.9 generally prohibits a later representation in the **same or a substantially related matter** with **materially adverse interests** unless the former client gives informed consent confirmed in writing. Do not assume time alone removes the connection or duties.

points.title: Information duties survive
points.text: Former-client information generally cannot be revealed except as the rules permit or require. The **generally known** exception in Rule 1.9(c)(1) concerns using information to the former client’s disadvantage; it is not a broad permission to reveal it. Public availability is not automatically the same as generally known.

sections.example: Thistle previously handled a merchant’s confidential licensing strategy. An opponent now wants her help attacking the same license. She must examine substantial relationship, adversity, information, and valid consent before accepting—not simply declare the old engagement closed.
tips: Locate the conflict first; then ask whether it is **consentable**.
The former-client **use** rule and **disclosure** rule are separate.

terms.definition: A conflict in which representation is opposed to another current client’s interests in the relevant sense.
A significant restriction on professional judgment or service due to other duties or interests.
A connection sufficient under Rule 1.9, including relevant risks from confidential information obtained in the former work.

sections.comicCaption: Loyalty follows former clients, and consent works only when the conflict is consentable.

sections.title: Fees, nonlawyers & independent judgment
sections.tagline: Follow the money without surrendering the judgment.

points.title: No outside control
points.text: Rule 5.4 protects **professional independence** through limits on sharing legal fees with nonlawyers, legal-service partnerships, and ownership or control, subject to stated exceptions. A permitted third-party payer cannot direct legal judgment. Under Rule 1.8(f), third-party compensation also requires **informed client consent**, independence, and protection of information.

points.title: Different fee divisions
points.text: Rule 1.5(e) permits division between lawyers in different firms only if the division is **proportional to services or each assumes joint responsibility**, the client agrees to the arrangement including each share and the agreement is **confirmed in writing**, and the total fee is reasonable. A pure referral fee without satisfying the requirements is not automatically proper.

points.title: Defined exceptions, not a blanket ban
points.text: Rule 5.4 allows specified arrangements such as qualifying employee compensation or retirement plans, including profit sharing, certain deceased-lawyer payments, and sharing court-awarded fees with a qualifying nonprofit. Analyze the actual exception. Jurisdictional departures from the Model Rule exist; do not generalize one state’s structure to all others.

sections.example: A woodland guild pays Thistle to represent a member. Payment does not make the guild the client or authorize it to dictate settlement. Thistle needs the required consent and must protect the member’s information and her own professional judgment.
tips: Identify whether the recipient is **another lawyer, an employee, a nonprofit, or an outside referrer**.
Who pays the bill is not necessarily **who controls the representation**.

terms.definition: The lawyer’s ability to exercise legal judgment free from prohibited outside control.
The responsibility assumed by lawyers sharing a fee under Rule 1.5(e), with meaning informed by the rule and applicable law.
Someone other than the client who pays for the client’s legal services.

sections.comicCaption: Keep client property safe and independent judgment free from outside pressure.

sections.title: Advertising, solicitation & public-interest advocacy
sections.tagline: How you approach someone matters.

points.title: Truthful communication
points.text: Rule 7.1 prohibits **false or misleading communications** about legal services, including material omissions. Truthful advertising has constitutional protection, but that does not license guaranteed outcomes, misleading comparisons, or improper pressure.

points.title: Targeted live pitches
points.text: Rule 7.3 addresses an offer directed to a specific person known or reasonably understood to need legal services in a particular matter. **Live person-to-person solicitation** significantly motivated by **pecuniary gain** is generally barred unless a stated relationship, lawyer, or routine-business-user exception applies. Letters, email, and texts that can readily be disregarded are treated differently from live pressure.

points.title: Exceptions do not permit harassment
points.text: A target’s expressed wish not to be solicited, coercion, duress, or harassment remains a bar under Rule 7.3(c). Nonprofit political and civil-rights outreach has important **speech and association protections**. Distinguish protected advocacy from a commercial personal pitch, then apply the actual rule and local requirements.

sections.example: Rowan sends an accurate public notice about services. Thistle offers free assistance through a civil-rights organization. A third lawyer corners an injured stranger to seek a paid engagement. The medium, target, motive, relationship, and pressure make these different problems.
tips: Use five facts: **target, need, medium, motive, relationship**.
Even an otherwise permitted contact must stop when the person says **do not solicit me**.

terms.definition: A lawyer-initiated offer to a specific person known or reasonably known to need legal services in a particular matter.
A money-making motive; Rule 7.3 asks whether it is a significant motive for the live solicitation.
Litigation-related activity tied to political expression and association, illustrated by Button and Primus.

sections.comicCaption: Public messages must be truthful; direct outreach has special limits and public-interest exceptions.

sections.title: The organization as client
sections.tagline: Separate the entity from its officers.

points.title: Identity
points.text: The lawyer represents the organization acting through constituents; an officer is not automatically a personal client. Give an Upjohn warning when interests may diverge.

points.title: Escalation
points.text: When an officer acts in a way likely to substantially injure the entity, Rule 1.13 calls for referral to higher authority, ordinarily the board; external disclosure is a narrow last resort.

points.title: Joint work
points.text: Separate representation of the entity and an officer requires Rule 1.7 analysis, consent where possible, and an exit plan.

sections.example: A general counsel interviews the CFO about possible accounting fraud. The lawyer explains whom she represents before the CFO reveals private facts.
tips: Name the client and decision maker.
Check internal reporting, then the limited outside disclosure path.

terms.definition: An officer, director, or employee through whom the entity acts
Notice that organization counsel represents the entity and the entity controls the privilege
Referral to a higher organizational authority when required by Rule 1.13

sections.comicCaption: The castle is the client. Officers speak for it but are not automatically separate clients.

sections.title: Diminished capacity & protective action
sections.tagline: Preserve the relationship as far as possible.

points.title: Normal relationship
points.text: Maintain an ordinary lawyer client relationship as far as reasonably possible, even when capacity is impaired.

points.title: Protective action
points.text: If the client has diminished capacity, faces substantial physical, financial, or other harm, and cannot adequately act, Rule 1.14 permits reasonably necessary protective steps.

points.title: Disclosure
points.text: Reveal only information reasonably necessary to protect the client; a family member or guardian may help, but an adverse third party may not.

sections.example: A client with dementia signs a transfer after a relative pressures her. The lawyer first assesses her wishes and capacity, then considers limited protective action.
tips: Identify actual harm and inability to act.
Keep disclosure and intervention proportional.

terms.definition: Limited ability to make adequately considered decisions
Reasonably necessary steps to safeguard an impaired client
Reveal no more than reasonably necessary for protection

sections.comicCaption: Listen to the client first. Protective action must be necessary and proportionate.

sections.title: Discipline, reporting & Kansas procedure
sections.tagline: Licensing and discipline are distinct from civil liability.

points.title: Admission and candor
points.text: Rule 8.1 bars knowingly false material statements or failures to respond to lawful admissions and disciplinary demands, subject to Rule 1.6.

points.title: Reporting
points.text: Rule 8.3 requires reporting known misconduct that raises a substantial question about honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness; protected Rule 1.6 information is excepted.

points.title: Choice of law
points.text: Rule 8.5 separates disciplinary authority from the applicable conduct rule; tribunal conduct generally uses the tribunal jurisdiction, other conduct uses predominant effect.

points.title: Kansas process
points.text: Review Kansas Supreme Court Rules 202–225 for investigation, hearing, review, sanctions, and reinstatement. Distinguish discipline from fee or malpractice remedies.

sections.example: A lawyer sees a colleague steal trust funds. She assesses the knowledge and substantial question thresholds, confidentiality, and reporting channel.
tips: Ask who licenses and disciplines.
Apply the Rule 8.5 choice-of-law test before deciding the rule.

terms.definition: Serious doubt about honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness
Jurisdiction empowered to regulate lawyer conduct
Place with the strongest expected effect of conduct for Rule 8.5

sections.comicCaption: Discipline has its own forum, reporting thresholds, and choice-of-law rules.

sections.title: Fees, retainers & safekeeping property
sections.tagline: Reasonableness and accounting continue after signature.

points.title: Fee formation
points.text: Rule 1.5 requires a reasonable fee and timely communication of basis or rate, preferably in writing; contingency agreements have specific writing and content requirements and subject matter limits.

points.title: Property
points.text: Rule 1.15 requires segregation, records, prompt notice and delivery, and preservation of disputed funds while distributing undisputed amounts.

points.title: Special transactions
points.text: Financial assistance, business deals, gifts, and fee sharing require different Rule 1.8 tests; do not collapse them into one consent rule.

points.title: Awards
points.text: Statutory fee awards and waivers may differ from contractual client fees; analyze the governing statute and settlement terms.

sections.example: A client disputes $2,000 of a $10,000 trust balance. Counsel promptly pays the uncontested $8,000 and safeguards the rest until resolution.
tips: Calculate whether the fee is reasonable.
Separate earned fees from client property and disputed funds.

terms.definition: Segregated account for client or third party funds
Compensation dependent on outcome and subject to writing and matter limits
Property held separate until entitlement is resolved

sections.comicCaption: Keep client money apart, deliver undisputed funds, and preserve the amount in dispute.

sections.title: Attorney–client privilege & work product
sections.tagline: Different protections, different waiver tests.

points.title: Confidentiality
points.text: Rule 1.6 is an ethical duty covering information relating to representation; it is broader than evidentiary privilege.

points.title: Privilege
points.text: The attorney–client privilege generally protects confidential communications seeking or giving legal advice; the client holds and may waive it. Federal Rule of Evidence 501 determines source of privilege law.

points.title: Corporate communications
points.text: Upjohn rejects a simple control group limit. Examine employee communications made for corporate legal advice under direction, confidentiality, and subject matter.

points.title: Work product
points.text: FRCP 26(b)(3) protects material prepared because of litigation, with qualified discovery for ordinary work product and stronger protection for mental impressions.

points.title: Exceptions
points.text: Analyze crime–fraud, waiver, common interest, and other limits independently; facts themselves do not become privileged.

sections.example: An internal report quotes employee interviews for counsel’s legal advice. Identify each communication, holder, purpose, and whether litigation was anticipated.
tips: Classify each item: ethical secrecy, privilege, or work product.
Ask who can waive and what exception applies.

terms.definition: Evidence rule shielding qualifying confidential legal advice communications
Litigation preparation material protected under Rule 26(b)(3)
Exception for communications furthering future or ongoing wrongdoing

sections.comicCaption: Ask who holds the privilege, whether legal advice was sought, and why a document was prepared.

sections.title: Current-client conflicts
sections.tagline: Direct adversity and material limitation are separate paths.

points.title: Identify
points.text: Rule 1.7 covers direct adversity and significant risk that representation will be materially limited by duties to another client, former client, third person, or personal interest.

points.title: Consentability
points.text: Even with informed written consent, counsel needs reasonable belief in competent diligent representation, no legal prohibition, and no opposing claims between clients in the same litigation.

points.title: Consent
points.text: Explain reasonably available alternatives and material risks; obtain each affected client’s informed consent confirmed in writing.

points.title: Screening
points.text: A private firm’s screen ordinarily does not cure a nonconsentable current-client conflict under the Model Rules.

sections.example: A firm sues its current client on an unrelated matter. Direct adversity arises even without shared confidential information.
tips: Check adversity, then material limitation.
Run every Rule 1.7(b) condition before asking for consent.

terms.definition: Representation directly opposed to a current client
Significant risk other duties or interests restrict the lawyer
Agreement after adequate disclosure of material risks and alternatives

sections.comicCaption: Direct adversity can exist even when the two matters seem unrelated.

sections.title: Multiple clients & aggregate settlements
sections.tagline: One lawyer cannot promise secrecy inside a joint representation.

points.title: Common representation
points.text: Explain shared information, privilege implications, limits of confidentiality between joint clients, and what happens if interests split.

points.title: Aggregate settlement
points.text: Rule 1.8(g) requires each client’s informed consent in a writing signed by the client after disclosure of all claims or pleas and each participant’s part.

points.title: Allocation
points.text: Client autonomy over settlement persists for each participant; one majority vote cannot bind the minority without proper consent.

sections.example: Five plaintiffs want to settle together. Counsel discloses the total and each proposed share to all five and obtains signed informed consent from each.
tips: Identify who decides settlement.
Ask whether every affected client received every allocation and signed.

terms.definition: Package settlement covering multiple clients
One lawyer representing clients with aligned or potentially diverging interests
Distribution of settlement value among clients

sections.comicCaption: Every client needs the complete allocation before consenting to an aggregate settlement.

sections.title: Personal interests, gifts & lawyer as witness
sections.tagline: The lawyer’s own stake can constrain the client.

points.title: Business deals
points.text: Rule 1.8(a) calls for fair and reasonable terms in writing, written advice to seek independent counsel and reasonable opportunity, and informed written consent.

points.title: Gifts and assistance
points.text: Rule 1.8 limits soliciting substantial gifts and financial assistance, with narrow permitted litigation costs and indigent-client aid.

points.title: Witness
points.text: Rule 3.7 generally bars acting as advocate at trial when likely a necessary witness, subject to specific exceptions; firm colleagues may sometimes continue.

points.title: Risk
points.text: A fee, family tie, reputation, or financial stake can create a Rule 1.7(a)(2) material limitation.

sections.example: A lawyer proposes taking stock in a client startup for fees. Disclose the valuation, alternatives, written advice about independent counsel, and obtain written consent if the transaction is permissible.
tips: Separate Rule 1.8’s specific rule from Rule 1.7.
Identify any trial witness issue under Rule 3.7.

terms.definition: Lawyer client deal subject to Rule 1.8(a)
Trial witness whose testimony materially matters and is not readily replaced
Material limitation caused by lawyer’s own interests

sections.comicCaption: Your own stake or testimony can limit your ability to advocate for the client.

sections.title: Former clients & government service
sections.tagline: Substantial relationship and confidential information shape the boundaries.

points.title: Former clients
points.text: Rule 1.9 bars materially adverse representation in the same or substantially related matter without former client informed written consent; protected information cannot be misused.

points.title: Imputation
points.text: Rule 1.10 generally attributes a lawyer’s conflicts to a firm with defined departures, including a qualifying screen for certain lateral former-client matters.

points.title: Government
points.text: Rule 1.11 has tailored rules for former and current government lawyers, including personal and substantial participation and written agency consent or screening where allowed.

points.title: Comparison
points.text: Distinguish a lawyer’s personal prior work from a whole firm’s work and from a current-client conflict.

sections.example: An attorney who personally handled a permit case at an agency joins a firm challenging the permit. Analyze personal substantial participation and Rule 1.11 screening and notice.
tips: Find the earlier client or agency and matter.
Ask same/substantially related, adversity, and applicable screen.

terms.definition: Matters sharing the same transaction or a substantial risk of material confidential information
Attribution of one lawyer’s conflict to firm colleagues
Meaningful involvement in a specific government matter

sections.comicCaption: Leave former matters and government files behind unless the conflict rules permit the new role.

sections.title: Neutrals & criminal defense conflicts
sections.tagline: Prior roles and joint defense can narrow loyalty.

points.title: Neutral role
points.text: Rule 2.4 requires explaining to unrepresented parties that the neutral does not represent them when confusion is reasonable.

points.title: Former neutral
points.text: Rule 1.12 restricts representing anyone in a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as judge, arbitrator, mediator, or other neutral absent informed written consent; screening may protect a firm.

points.title: Criminal joint representation
points.text: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 44(c) calls for prompt inquiry into joint representation and advice on independent counsel; conflicts may justify separate lawyers even if defendants prefer one.

sections.example: A mediator joins a firm asked to represent one party in the same dispute. Check Rule 1.12 consent and whether the firm can screen and give notice.
tips: Identify earlier role and same matter.
For criminal co-defendants, assess divergent plea and testimony incentives.

terms.definition: Lawyer assisting parties without representing either
Federal criminal court examination of joint representation
Isolation from participation and fees with required notice where permitted

sections.comicCaption: A neutral serves neither side; criminal co-defendants may need separate counsel.

sections.title: Meritorious claims & candor to the tribunal
sections.tagline: Advocacy has a floor and a correction duty.

points.title: Merit
points.text: Rule 3.1 bars frivolous claims or defenses, though criminal defense may require prosecution to establish every element.

points.title: Candor
points.text: Rule 3.3 prohibits false statements of law or fact and knowing use of false evidence; a lawyer must take reasonable remedial measures, possibly disclosure despite Rule 1.6.

points.title: Duration
points.text: The candor duties continue to conclusion of a proceeding; ex parte proceedings require disclosure of material facts needed for informed decision.

points.title: Tension
points.text: Separate client confidentiality from the overriding tribunal duty in Rule 3.3(c).

sections.example: A witness admits testimony was false after the hearing. Counsel remonstrates, seeks correction, and follows Rule 3.3 if private correction fails.
tips: Was the falsehood knowing and material?
List reasonable remedial steps in order.

terms.definition: Position lacking a nonfrivolous basis under Rule 3.1
Steps to correct false evidence or statements
Proceeding where opposing party is absent

sections.comicCaption: Correct known falsehoods to the tribunal through the required remedial steps.

sections.title: Evidence & fairness to the other side
sections.tagline: Preserve proof, avoid fabrication, and deal fairly.

points.title: Evidence
points.text: Rule 3.4 bars unlawful obstruction or destruction of evidence, falsification, improper witness inducements, and knowing disobedience of tribunal obligations except open refusal on validity grounds.

points.title: Witness preparation
points.text: Preparing a witness is permitted; coaching false testimony or paying for content is not.

points.title: Nonadjudicative advocacy
points.text: Rule 3.9 requires disclosure of representative capacity and conformity with selected candor and fairness duties before legislative or administrative bodies.

points.title: Misconduct
points.text: Rule 8.4 reaches dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, and certain conduct prejudicial to justice.

sections.example: Counsel discovers an unfavorable document subject to a preservation hold. She preserves it and litigates privilege or production, rather than deleting it.
tips: Identify the item and preservation duty.
Distinguish legitimate preparation from shaping false evidence.

terms.definition: Improper destruction or alteration of relevant evidence
Payment or benefit that can improperly influence testimony
Government decision process outside adjudication

sections.comicCaption: Preserve evidence and test admissibility without altering the proof.

sections.title: Witnesses, jurors & nonclients
sections.tagline: Contacts turn on whom the lawyer represents.

points.title: Witnesses
points.text: Rule 3.4 and applicable procedural rules govern requests to nonclients, payments, and evidence access; do not induce false testimony.

points.title: Jurors
points.text: Rule 3.5 limits improper contact with judges, jurors, and prospective jurors; post-discharge contact still has defined boundaries.

points.title: Represented and unrepresented people
points.text: Rules 4.2 and 4.3 distinguish represented persons from unrepresented people; clarify role and avoid legal advice beyond obtaining counsel when interests conflict.

sections.example: An investigator interviews a witness who has counsel for this matter. The lawyer pauses to assess Rule 4.2 before any substantive contact.
tips: Is the person represented in this matter?
Did contact involve a juror, witness payment, or tribunal official?

terms.definition: Person with counsel in the matter within Rule 4.2
Person without counsel to whom Rule 4.3 applies
Improper communication with a juror outside authorized process

sections.comicCaption: Know when a witness, juror, or nonclient is off limits for contact.

sections.title: Publicity, decorum & improper influence
sections.tagline: Protect proceedings from advocacy outside the record.

points.title: Trial publicity
points.text: Rule 3.6 restricts extrajudicial statements by participating lawyers that they know or should know have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding, with safe categories and a response exception.

points.title: Decorum
points.text: Rule 3.5 prohibits improper influence and disruption of a tribunal.

points.title: Arguments
points.text: Opening and closing must stay within evidence and permissible inferences; attorney opinion or inflammatory appeals risk discipline and reversal.

points.title: Bias
points.text: Rule 8.4(g), where adopted, addresses harassment or discrimination in law-related activities, subject to its terms and jurisdictional variation.

sections.example: A prosecutor discusses an unadmitted confession on television before trial. Assess likely prejudice, Rule 3.6 limits, and possible remedial action.
tips: Ask if a proceeding is pending and likely prejudiced.
Separate court contact, speech, and trial argument.

terms.definition: Extrajudicial speech potentially prejudicing an adjudication
Prohibited attempt to affect a tribunal or juror
Orderly conduct required in proceedings

sections.comicCaption: Speak publicly without materially prejudicing the proceeding or pressuring the tribunal.

sections.title: Judicial impartiality, recusal & outside activity
sections.tagline: A judge must protect both fairness and its appearance.

points.title: Canon 1
points.text: Judges must uphold independence, integrity, and impartiality and avoid impropriety and its appearance.

points.title: Canon 2
points.text: Duties include faithful performance, impartiality, restrictions on ex parte communications, public comment, campaign-related behavior, and disqualification when impartiality might reasonably be questioned.

points.title: Canon 3
points.text: Extrajudicial activities, gifts, financial activity, and compensation have limits; the Code allows some civic and educational activity with safeguards.

points.title: Recusal
points.text: Analyze objective grounds, required disclosure, and whether remittal is allowed. Judicial rulings alone ordinarily require more than disagreement.

sections.example: A judge learns a close relative has a financial stake in one litigant. The judge discloses the connection and applies disqualification and remittal rules.
tips: Name the Code provision and decision point.
Distinguish actual bias, appearance, and permitted outside activity.

terms.definition: Judge’s withdrawal from a proceeding where disqualification is required
Communication with a judge outside the other parties’ participation
Permitted waiver of certain disqualification grounds after prescribed disclosure

sections.comicCaption: A judge steps aside when impartiality might reasonably be questioned.

sections.title: Criticism of judges, civility & bias
sections.tagline: Speech protection coexists with truthfulness and courtroom rules.

points.title: Judicial criticism
points.text: Rule 8.2 bars statements about a judge or candidate’s qualifications or integrity made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth.

points.title: Court conduct
points.text: Rule 3.5 and court orders address disruption and decorum; distinguish sharp advocacy from disobedience.

points.title: Bias and harassment
points.text: Rule 8.4(g) requires careful attention to jurisdictional adoption and the connection to law practice; also consider Rule 8.4(d).

sections.example: After an adverse ruling, counsel posts a factual accusation of corruption without checking the readily available record. Analyze knowledge or reckless disregard.
tips: Identify speech, audience, factual basis, and mental state.
Keep state adoption of Rule 8.4(g) explicit.

terms.definition: Serious doubts about truth ignored when making a factual accusation
Fitness and honesty protected by Rule 8.2
Behavioral requirements during proceedings

sections.comicCaption: Check the factual basis for criticism and keep the courtroom free of bias.

sections.title: Prosecutors: charging, disclosure & innocence
sections.tagline: The prosecutor seeks justice, not only convictions.

points.title: Charging and rights
points.text: Rule 3.8(a) bars prosecuting a charge not supported by probable cause; other provisions protect counsel access and limit waivers by unrepresented accused people.

points.title: Disclosure
points.text: Rule 3.8(d) requires timely disclosure of evidence tending to negate guilt or mitigate offense, plus sentencing mitigation; constitutional Brady doctrine has its own materiality framework.

points.title: Publicity
points.text: Rule 3.8(f) limits prejudicial extrajudicial comments and asks prosecutors to restrain associated personnel.

points.title: After conviction
points.text: Rule 3.8(g) and (h) set separate duties for new credible material evidence and clear convincing evidence of wrongful conviction, with jurisdictional variations.

sections.example: A prosecutor receives exculpatory lab results. She promptly assesses disclosure under Rule 3.8(d), Brady, and any court order rather than awaiting trial strategy.
tips: Separate ethics timing from constitutional remedy.
For later evidence, distinguish credible/material from clear/convincing.

terms.definition: Minimum basis required by Rule 3.8(a) to prosecute
Information tending to negate guilt
Rule 3.8(g) and (h) responses to evidence of wrongful conviction

sections.comicCaption: The prosecutor’s duty of disclosure serves justice beyond a win-loss tally.

sections.title: Pro bono, appointments & special responsibility
sections.tagline: Professional obligations extend beyond paying clients.

points.title: Pro bono
points.text: Rule 6.1 states an aspirational responsibility, commonly 50 hours annually, with substantial service to persons of limited means or qualifying organizations.

points.title: Appointments
points.text: Rule 6.2 limits refusal of tribunal appointment to good cause, including likely Rule violation, unreasonable financial burden, or repugnance severe enough to impair representation.

points.title: Special responsibilities
points.text: Review law reform, access to justice, professional institutions, and the state-specific disciplinary framework; ethical ideals and enforceable rules are different categories.

points.title: Review method
points.text: For each problem: client, duty, trigger, exception, remedy, and jurisdiction.

sections.example: A lawyer asked to take a difficult appointed case evaluates competence, conflicts, and good cause rather than refusing solely because the client is unpopular.
tips: Distinguish aspiration from discipline.
Tie refusal to a Rule 6.2 good-cause ground.

terms.definition: Voluntary legal service for public good under Rule 6.1
Representation assigned by a tribunal
Permissible reason under Rule 6.2 to decline an appointment

sections.comicCaption: Public service and careful appointments help keep the courthouse open to all.

cases.name: Birbrower, Montalbano, Condon & Frank v. Superior Court
cases.facts: New York lawyers performed substantial California legal work without California authorization and sought their fees.
cases.issue: Could they recover for unauthorized California services?
cases.holding: They could not recover for unauthorized work but could seek fees for severable lawful work elsewhere.
cases.reasoning: The nature and extent of contacts mattered; legal practice was not confined to court appearances or physical presence.
cases.trap: This applies California law at the time. Check modern local authorization and arbitration rules before applying its result to current facts.

cases.name: Strickland v. Washington
cases.facts: A capital defendant challenged counsel’s investigation and presentation of mitigation.
cases.issue: What ordinarily establishes constitutionally ineffective assistance?
cases.holding: The Court required deficient performance and prejudice and rejected relief on the facts.
cases.reasoning: Reasonableness is assessed with deference and context; prejudice requires a reasonable probability of a different result sufficient to undermine confidence.
cases.trap: Do not substitute an ethics violation, a poor outcome, or hindsight for the two-part constitutional inquiry.

cases.name: Lerner v. Laufer
cases.facts: A lawyer reviewed a mediated divorce agreement under an explained limited engagement that excluded independent financial investigation.
cases.issue: Was the scope limitation valid, and did it defeat the malpractice claim?
cases.holding: The court upheld the limited scope and affirmed judgment for the lawyer; it disapproved language attempting to prevent malpractice litigation.
cases.reasoning: The agreed task defined the duty, and causation was also lacking because the client later had a renewed opportunity to litigate.
cases.trap: This New Jersey decision illustrates the scope/liability distinction. Apply the current Model Rule’s independent-representation requirement separately to a prospective liability limit.

cases.name: Jones v. Barnes
cases.facts: Appellate counsel selected promising issues instead of briefing every nonfrivolous issue requested by the accused.
cases.issue: Did the Constitution require all requested nonfrivolous arguments?
cases.holding: No; counsel could exercise professional judgment in selecting issues.
cases.reasoning: Effective advocacy often requires focusing the appeal rather than diluting it with every possible contention.
cases.trap: The client retains fundamental decisions, including whether to appeal; counsel still owes competent service and communication.

cases.name: McCoy v. Louisiana
cases.facts: Counsel conceded guilt in a capital trial over the defendant’s express insistence on innocence, hoping to avoid a death sentence.
cases.issue: Could counsel override that objective as a strategic choice?
cases.holding: No. The violation of client autonomy was structural error requiring a new trial.
cases.reasoning: Maintaining innocence was a client-controlled objective, distinct from technical tactics or ordinary ineffective-assistance analysis.
cases.trap: The express objection matters. Do not assume every concession in every case triggers this holding.

cases.name: Bates v. State Bar of Arizona
cases.facts: Lawyers advertised prices for routine legal services in a newspaper and faced discipline under a broad advertising restriction.
cases.issue: Could the state impose that blanket ban on truthful price advertising?
cases.holding: The First Amendment protected the advertising at issue against the blanket ban.
cases.reasoning: Accurate information about legal services can help the public make informed choices.
cases.trap: Misleading advertising and improper solicitation remain regulable; the decision is not immunity for every marketing claim.

cases.name: Ohralik v. Ohio State Bar Association
cases.facts: A lawyer personally approached accident victims to obtain paid representation.
cases.issue: Could the state discipline this commercial in-person solicitation?
cases.holding: Yes. The First Amendment did not prevent discipline in these circumstances.
cases.reasoning: Live personal pressure and the risks of overreaching supported prophylactic regulation.
cases.trap: Compare medium, motive, and relationship. The decision does not treat all written or nonprofit outreach identically.

cases.name: In re Primus
cases.facts: An ACLU-associated lawyer sent a letter offering free legal help in a matter connected to the organization’s civil-rights work.
cases.issue: Could the state punish this activity as ordinary improper solicitation?
cases.holding: Not on the justification and circumstances presented; the discipline violated protected expression and association.
cases.reasoning: The outreach advanced political and associational objectives rather than the commercial pressure present in Ohralik.
cases.trap: The protection is contextual. It does not authorize deception, coercion, or harassment.

cases.name: NAACP v. Button
cases.facts: Virginia applied solicitation restrictions to the NAACP’s efforts to connect civil-rights litigants with lawyers.
cases.issue: Could the state suppress that litigation-related advocacy through the challenged restriction?
cases.holding: The Court held the challenged application unconstitutional.
cases.reasoning: Litigation was a means of political expression and association, requiring carefully confined regulation.
cases.trap: Identify the expressive and associational context instead of assuming every effort to locate clients is identical.

cases.name: Florida Bar v. Brumbaugh
cases.facts: A nonlawyer sold typing help and divorce forms and gave customers advice on completing them.
cases.issue: Where does clerical form assistance become unauthorized legal practice?
cases.holding: The Florida Supreme Court enjoined individualized legal advice while allowing sale of forms and purely clerical typing.
cases.reasoning: Applying law to a person’s facts crosses the line from transmitting information to exercising legal judgment.
cases.trap: Jurisdictions draw UPL boundaries differently; do not treat every form service as practice of law.

cases.name: In re Robbins
cases.facts: A lawyer’s dealings with a person raised questions about whether representation began and whether a personal interest impaired judgment.
cases.issue: When does conduct create a lawyer–client relationship, and what duties follow?
cases.holding: The D.C. Court of Appeals affirmed discipline including a sixty-day suspension for misconduct in the relationship.
cases.reasoning: The client’s reasonable understanding and the lawyer’s conduct matter more than a formal label.
cases.trap: Use the case’s D.C. rules and facts; a preliminary conversation alone does not always create full representation.

cases.name: Whiting v. Lacara
cases.facts: Counsel sought to withdraw when the client’s insistence on conduct threatened counsel’s professional obligations.
cases.issue: Was refusal to permit withdrawal proper?
cases.holding: The Second Circuit permitted immediate appellate review and held denial of withdrawal was an abuse of discretion.
cases.reasoning: A lawyer should not be forced into a position that would compromise professional obligations or expose counsel to discipline.
cases.trap: Withdrawal still requires tribunal permission when required and reasonable protection of the client.

cases.name: Upjohn Co. v. United States
cases.facts: Company counsel investigated payments and interviewed employees for legal advice.
cases.issue: Is corporate privilege restricted to communications by the corporate control group?
cases.holding: The Supreme Court rejected the control-group test and protected qualifying employee communications.
cases.reasoning: Legal advice requires information from employees who know the facts; counsel’s work product also receives protection.
cases.trap: The underlying facts are not privileged, and privilege depends on purpose and confidentiality.

cases.name: Evans v. Jeff D.
cases.facts: A class settlement offered relief while conditioning it on waiver of statutory attorney fees.
cases.issue: Could counsel accept a fee waiver as part of a settlement under the civil-rights fee statute?
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held the district court could approve the negotiated fee waiver on the case facts.
cases.reasoning: The fee statute did not prohibit the waiver; client settlement interests and counsel’s fee interests required careful attention.
cases.trap: Do not assume a fee award belongs to counsel independently of settlement authority or that every waiver is ethically unproblematic.

cases.name: Brady v. Maryland
cases.facts: The prosecution withheld a co-defendant’s statement relevant to punishment.
cases.issue: What constitutional duty applies to favorable prosecution evidence?
cases.holding: Suppression of favorable material evidence upon request violated due process.
cases.reasoning: Fairness limits the prosecution’s use of its superior access to evidence.
cases.trap: Constitutional materiality and Rule 3.8(d)’s ethical disclosure obligation are distinct tests.

cases.name: Bordenkircher v. Hayes
cases.facts: A prosecutor offered a plea and warned that refusing it would lead to a more serious supported charge.
cases.issue: Did that charging decision violate due process in plea bargaining?
cases.holding: The Supreme Court found no due-process violation where the defendant was free to accept or reject the offer and the charge had probable cause.
cases.reasoning: Plea bargaining permits hard choices within lawful charging bounds.
cases.trap: Do not read this as permission to bring charges lacking probable cause or to violate disclosure duties.

cases.name: Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co.
cases.facts: A litigant’s principal supported a judicial election with extraordinary spending before the judge heard that litigant’s appeal.
cases.issue: Did due process require recusal despite state procedures?
cases.holding: The Supreme Court required recusal because the extreme circumstances created a serious risk of actual bias.
cases.reasoning: An objective probability of bias in an exceptional election context can cross the constitutional floor.
cases.trap: The due-process floor is narrower than ordinary judicial ethics recusal rules.

cases.name: Williams v. Pennsylvania
cases.facts: A state chief justice later reviewed a death-penalty case in which he had earlier participated as district attorney.
cases.issue: Can a judge hear a case after significant personal involvement in a critical prosecution decision?
cases.reasoning: A judge’s earlier significant personal prosecutorial role creates an intolerable risk of bias.
cases.trap: Separate constitutional disqualification from the broader Model Code and state recusal provisions.
